--- title: "Week 10 Exercises" distributed: 2026-10-27 show-hints: true --- ## Simulate and Recover; Ordered Logit {ref="sim-recover-ordered"} One important way to test and develop your understandings of statistical models and quantities of interest is to *simulate* a fake data set with known true quantity of interest (e.g., coefficients or first difference) and then *recover* that quantity of interest through your estimation procedure. - Week 9 did this for logit: [Simulate and Recover; Logit](wk09-exercises.html#ex-8). Do this for the ordered logit model in the [notes](https://pos5747.github.io/notes/wk06/03-ordered-logit.html). As your quantity of interest, use $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ when `income` equals 1.5 and `x2` equals `"Label 1"`. 1. First, simulate a fake data set with known cutpoints, coefficients, and quantity of interest. The code below handles this. Notice that the linear predictor `eta` has no intercept. The cutpoints `alpha` take its place. 1. Second, use `MASS::polr()` to fit an ordered logit model to the fake data. Are the true cutpoints and coefficients inside their 95% confidence intervals? (`polr()` calls the cutpoints "Intercepts" and labels them `1|2`, `2|3`, and `3|4`.) 1. Third, use `predictions()` to recover the true quantity of interest. Is the true value inside the 95% CI? 1. Fourth, adapt the code to compute the true first difference in $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ as `income` moves from −1.5 to 1.5 (with `x2` equal to `"Label 1"`). Then recover it with `comparisons()`. 1. Fifth, refit the model with `brm(family = cumulative("logit"))`. Recover the cutpoints, the coefficients, and the first difference. Compare with `polr()` and the truth. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # --- simulate a fake data set --- # set seed for reproducibility set.seed(1234) # set sample size n <- 10000 # needs to be large enough so that CI isn't super wide # create explanatory variables ## numeric variable; six brackets, like income in the anes data income <- sample(c(-2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5), size = n, replace = TRUE) ## qualitative variable x2 <- sample(c("Label 1", "Label 2"), size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)) # about 75% will be "Label 1" # create cutpoints and coefficients alpha <- c(-1, 0.5, 2) # J - 1 = 3 cutpoints, so J = 4 categories b1 <- 0.4 b2 <- 1 # linear predictor; no intercept! eta <- b1*income + b2*(x2 == "Label 2") # cumulative probabilities Pr(y <= j), j = 1, 2, 3 cp1 <- plogis(alpha[1] - eta) cp2 <- plogis(alpha[2] - eta) cp3 <- plogis(alpha[3] - eta) # category probabilities Pr(y = j), j = 1, 2, 3, 4; one row per observation p <- cbind(cp1, cp2 - cp1, cp3 - cp2, 1 - cp3) # simulate outcome for ordered logit model; one draw per observation y <- numeric(n) for (i in 1:n) { y[i] <- sample(1:4, size = 1, prob = p[i, ]) } # combine into data frame; y must be an ordered factor for polr() data <- data.frame(y = factor(y, ordered = TRUE), income, x2) # truth: Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1" eta_c <- b1*1.5 # x2 = "Label 1", so the b2 term is zero 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - eta_c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5249792 ``` ::: ::: ::: hint $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ is the sum of the probabilities of categories 3 and 4. - Week 6 added up category probabilities with `hypothesis`: [Red State, Blue State: Part 2(a)](wk06-exercises.html#ex-8), part 3. ::: ::: hint - `family = cumulative("logit")`. - `fixef()` labels the cutpoints `Intercept[1]`, `Intercept[2]`, and `Intercept[3]`. - The same `predictions()` and `comparisons()` calls work on the `brm()` fit. ::: ::: sol **Part 1** The true value of $\Pr(y \geq 3)$ is about 0.525. Notice that $\Pr(y \geq 3) = 1 - \Pr(y \leq 2) = 1 - \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_2 - \eta)$, so we only need the second cutpoint. **Part 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # fit ordered logit model fit <- MASS::polr(y ~ income + x2, data = data, Hess = TRUE) # estimates and 95% cis for the coefficients and the cutpoints est <- c(coef(fit), fit$zeta) se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))) cbind(truth = c(b1, b2, alpha), estimate = est, lower = est - 1.96*se, upper = est + 1.96*se) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth estimate lower upper income 0.4 0.4090809 0.3867683 0.4313935 x2Label 2 1.0 0.9227028 0.8392080 1.0061975 1|2 -1.0 -1.0002890 -1.0507747 -0.9498033 2|3 0.5 0.5110824 0.4638427 0.5583221 3|4 2.0 2.0179461 1.9557867 2.0801055 ``` ::: ::: All five true values are inside their 95% confidence intervals. The true value of `b2` (i.e., 1) is only barely inside its interval (about 0.84 to 1.01); across many simulated data sets, we'd expect the interval to miss the true value about 5% of the time. **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # recover Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1" predictions(fit, newdata = datagrid(income = 1.5, x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.526 0.00709 74.2 <0.001 Inf 0.512 0.54 Type: probs ``` ::: ::: The estimate is about 0.526, and the 95% CI runs from about 0.512 to 0.540. The true value (about 0.525) is inside the interval, as it usually will be. **Part 4** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # truth: fd in Pr(y >= 3) as income moves from -1.5 to 1.5; x2 = "Label 1" pr_hi <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*1.5) pr_lo <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*(-1.5)) pr_hi - pr_lo ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2752393 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # recover this fd comparisons(fit, variables = list(income = c(-1.5, 1.5)), newdata = datagrid(x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.28 0.00746 37.6 <0.001 1025.9 0.266 0.295 Type: probs ``` ::: ::: The true first difference is about 0.275. The estimate is about 0.280, and the 95% CI runs from about 0.266 to 0.295. The true value is inside the interval. **Part 5** ::: {.cell fit_deps='data'} ```{.r .cell-code} # fit the same ordered logit with brm() fit_brm_ordered <- brm(y ~ income + x2, data = data, family = cumulative("logit"), backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # posterior means and 95% credible intervals, next to the truth and polr() cbind(truth = c(alpha, b1, b2), polr = c(fit$zeta, coef(fit)), fixef(fit_brm_ordered)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth polr Estimate Q2.5 Q97.5 1|2 -1.0 -1.0002890 -1.0002781 -1.0502979 -0.9523978 2|3 0.5 0.5110824 0.5109043 0.4649223 0.5569903 3|4 2.0 2.0179461 2.0181554 1.9581049 2.0801383 income 0.4 0.4090809 0.4089016 0.3866045 0.4315740 x2Label 2 1.0 0.9227028 0.9223948 0.8429649 1.0034713 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # recover the fd with the brm() fit comparisons(fit_brm_ordered, variables = list(income = c(-1.5, 1.5)), newdata = datagrid(x2 = "Label 1"), hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypothesis Estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % b3+b4=0 0.28 0.266 0.295 Type: response ``` ::: ::: - Posterior means match `polr()` to about 0.001. All five true values are inside the 95% credible intervals. - First difference: 0.28 (95% CI from 0.266 to 0.295). Truth (0.275) is inside. - Same {marginaleffects} code for both fits. ::: ## Eight Schools {ref="eight-schools"} In my slides, I motivated hierarchical models with the "309 problem." There's a similar motivational problem called the "eight schools" problem. This example is worth studying carefully. 1. Read this blog post (by Phil Price) on Andrew Gelman's blog: "[Everything I need to know about Bayesian statistics, I learned in eight schools](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/01/21/everything-need-know-bayesian-statistics-learned-eight-schools/)." 1. Read the pp. 119-124 of [*BDA3*](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf) on the eight schools problem. 1. Run the R code [here](https://pos5747.github.io/files/wk10-eight-schools.R). Note that the notation in my Stan model differs from BDA3. 1. In the model, $\sigma$ captures the *similarity* of the treatment effects across school districts. I give this parameter a [half-Cauchy prior](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf) with a scale of 20. (See the note below.) How does changing the scale of the half-Cauchy prior in the Stan model affect the estimates of $\sigma$? a. Try setting the scale of the half-Cauchy to 5 instead of 20. a. Try setting it to 100. Hint: you can use `sigma_draws <- spread_draws(fit, sigma)` to get a convenient data frame of posterior simulations of $\sigma$. *Make sure you understand the basic eight schools example and can discuss it in parallel to the 309 example in the slides.* **So what's a half-Cauchy?** A Cauchy distribution is a location-scale *t* distribution with one degree of freedom. The *half-Cauchy* is centered at zero and *folded over*, so that it is just the rightward half. It has only a scale parameter that corresponds to something like the "expected" value of $\sigma$.^[The scale parameters of the Cauchy is also denoted as $\sigma$, so I just call it the "scale" here.] The expected value of the half-Cauchy does not exist, but the median equals the scale parameter. This is a useful *weakly informative* prior for variance parameters that capture similarity in hierarchical models. In this case, the student-level SAT scores range from 200 to 800, and the treatment effects are somewhere around a 10-point improvement. In the Stan model, $\sigma$ is the SD around that 10-point effect across schools. $\sigma = 20$ would be huge variation; $\sigma = 3$ or $\sigma = 5$ seem "about right." So I think of a half-Cauchy with a scale of 20 as a "weakly informative" prior that only rules out absurdly large values of $\sigma$ and gently encourages smaller rather than larger values. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: sol **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(cmdstanr) library(tidybayes) # eight-schools data; from my 2nd ed. of BDA on p. 140 est <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12) se_est <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18) J <- length(est) # the stan model from the script (centered), with the prior scale as data stan_code_centered <- " data { int J; vector[J] est; vector[J] se_est; real scale; // scale of the half-cauchy prior on sigma } parameters { real mu; real sigma; vector[J] theta; } model { mu ~ normal(0, 1000); sigma ~ cauchy(0, scale); theta ~ normal(mu, sigma); est ~ normal(theta, se_est); } " ``` ::: ::: {.cell fit_deps='["est","se_est","stan_code_centered"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} model_centered <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(stan_code_centered)) fit_centered <- model_centered$sample( data = list(J = J, est = est, se_est = se_est, scale = 20), seed = 123, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, iter_warmup = 2000, iter_sampling = 2000 ) # pull the draws and diagnostics into memory (cmdstanr keeps them in temp files) centered_summary <- fit_centered$summary(variables = c("mu", "sigma")) centered_diagnostics <- fit_centered$diagnostic_summary() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} centered_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 10 variable mean median sd mad q5 q95 rhat ess_bulk ess_tail 1 mu 7.88 8.08 4.96 4.66 -0.327 15.7 1.00 1426. 2649. 2 sigma 6.30 5.22 4.64 4.02 1.24 15.0 1.01 249. 75.9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} centered_diagnostics ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $num_divergent [1] 65 28 68 18 $num_max_treedepth [1] 0 0 0 0 $ebfmi [1] 0.3437584 0.2633397 0.2776665 0.3981525 ``` ::: ::: - Divergent transitions in every chain and low E-BFMI. The ESS for `sigma` is small. - A known problem with this model: when `sigma` is small, the `theta`s must sit close to `mu`, and the sampler can't move through that region. - The fix is the *non-centered* parameterization: sample standardized effects `z` and set `theta = mu + sigma * z`. Same model, easier posterior. **Part 4** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # non-centered version: same model, theta = mu + sigma * z stan_code_noncentered <- " data { int J; vector[J] est; vector[J] se_est; real scale; // scale of the half-cauchy prior on sigma } parameters { real mu; real sigma; vector[J] z; // standardized school effects } transformed parameters { vector[J] theta = mu + sigma * z; } model { mu ~ normal(0, 1000); sigma ~ cauchy(0, scale); z ~ std_normal(); // implies theta ~ normal(mu, sigma) est ~ normal(theta, se_est); } " ``` ::: ::: {.cell fit_deps='["est","se_est","stan_code_noncentered"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} model_noncentered <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(stan_code_noncentered)) # fit the model for one prior scale; return the draws of sigma and the divergences fit_scale <- function(scale) { fit <- model_noncentered$sample( data = list(J = J, est = est, se_est = se_est, scale = scale), seed = 123, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, iter_warmup = 2000, iter_sampling = 2000, adapt_delta = 0.95 ) tibble(sigma_draws = list(spread_draws(fit, sigma)), divergent = sum(fit$diagnostic_summary()$num_divergent)) } # one row per prior scale scale_fits <- tibble(scale = c(5, 20, 100)) |> mutate(fit = map(scale, fit_scale)) |> unnest(fit) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # posterior of sigma for each prior scale scale_fits |> unnest(sigma_draws) |> summarize(divergent = first(divergent), median = median(sigma), q05 = quantile(sigma, 0.05), q95 = quantile(sigma, 0.95), .by = scale) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 5 scale divergent median q05 q95 1 5 0 2.74 0.236 9.92 2 20 0 4.65 0.480 14.7 3 100 0 5.21 0.476 16.9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # posterior densities of sigma scale_fits |> unnest(sigma_draws) |> ggplot(aes(x = sigma, color = factor(scale))) + geom_density() + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 30)) + labs(x = "sigma", y = "Posterior density", color = "Scale of the\nhalf-Cauchy prior") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: - Larger scale, larger `sigma`: the posterior median and 95th percentile both rise as the scale goes from 5 to 100. - Eight schools say little about `sigma`, so the prior matters. - Scale 5 pulls `sigma` toward zero and the school effects toward `mu`. Scale 100 lets them spread out. ::: ## Feelings Toward Donald Trump {ref="trump-feelings"} The dataset [here](https://pos5747.github.io/files/anes-ft-groups.csv) from the 2016 ANES has data on feeling thermometer ratings of Donald Trump and a `social_group` variable that indicates a race-sex-degree triplet. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anes <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/anes-ft-groups.csv") |> glimpse() ``` ::: I'm interested in the feelings of each group toward Donald Trump. You can see that the sample averages and sample sizes vary a lot across the groups.^[Three of the *possible* groups have zero observations.] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tinytable) anes |> group_by(social_group) |> summarize(`Number of Respondents` = n(), `Sample Average` = mean(ft_donald_trump)) |> rename(`Social Group` = social_group) |> arrange(desc(`Number of Respondents`)) |> tt(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Use a hierarchical model to estimate the average for each group. ::: sol ::: {.cell fit_deps='anes'} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- ft_donald_trump ~ (1 | social_group) fit <- brm(f, data = anes, chains = 4, cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- predictions(fit, newdata = datagrid(social_group = unique)) p |> select(social_group, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) |> arrange(estimate) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` social_group Estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % Black; Female; College Degree 13.4 5.57744 21.1 Black; Male; College Degree 20.5 9.11882 31.7 Black; Female; No College Degree 21.9 16.65551 27.3 White; Other; College Degree 25.8 -0.00788 49.6 Other; Other; No College Degree 26.6 2.16845 49.0 Black; Male; No College Degree 26.8 20.70723 33.0 Other; Female; College Degree 27.0 20.70835 33.3 Other; Female; No College Degree 29.5 25.34214 33.8 White; Other; No College Degree 31.8 11.26984 52.7 White; Female; College Degree 33.8 31.08230 36.4 Other; Male; College Degree 35.8 29.99756 41.7 Other; Male; No College Degree 38.4 33.92532 42.9 White; Male; College Degree 42.3 39.54521 45.1 White; Female; No College Degree 52.4 50.11527 54.6 White; Male; No College Degree 56.5 54.04144 58.9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Red State, Blue State: Part 6 {ref="red-state-part-6"} - [Part 4](wk09-exercises.html#ex-10) fit a separate logit in each state. - Now fit one hierarchical model to all 50 states. Each state gets its own intercept, and the 50 intercepts come from a normal distribution. - This is the varying-intercept model behind Figure 3 of Gelman et al. (2007, p. 355) [[pdf](https://pos5747.github.io/notes/readings/Gelman2007.pdf)]. - `income` varies across voters within a state. `rs_state_median_income` varies only across states: state median household income, rescaled to mean 0 and SD 0.5 across the 50 states. - Same CES data as Part 4. The code below adds `rs_state_median_income`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load data; 50 states ces <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part4.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 48582 Columns: 5 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (2): state_name, state_abbr dbl (3): state_median_income, income, vote_rep ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # one row per state; rescale state income to mean 0 and sd 0.5 across the 50 states states <- ces |> distinct(state_name, state_abbr, state_median_income) |> mutate(rs_state_median_income = (state_median_income - mean(state_median_income)) / (2 * sd(state_median_income))) # add rescaled state income to the voters ces <- ces |> left_join(select(states, state_name, rs_state_median_income), by = "state_name") ``` ::: 1. Use `brm()` to fit the logit `vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name)`. Use `family = bernoulli`, `backend = "cmdstanr"`, `iter = 10000`, and `warmup = 2000`. Check R-hat and the ESS. 1. Use `predictions()` to compute Pr(Trump), with a 90% CI, for a voter in the middle income category (`income = 0`) in each state. Plot these 50 estimates and their CIs against `state_median_income`, labeled with the state abbreviations. 1. Add a line for a typical state (i.e., a state whose intercept is exactly what state income predicts). Use `predictions()` with `re_formula = NA` over a range of state incomes. 1. Interpret the coefficients on `income` and `rs_state_median_income`. Where does each show up in your plot? What is the vertical distance between a state's point and the line? 1. In Part 4, the effect of income differed across states (e.g., about 0.15 in Mississippi and about −0.08 in Oregon). Does the effect of income differ across states in this model? Why or why not? 1. Gelman et al. (2007) describe a paradox: richer voters lean Republican, but richer states lean Democratic. Does this model show the same paradox in 2024? ::: hint - Each state needs its own `rs_state_median_income` in the grid. - `grid <- mutate(states, income = 0)` gives one row per state. - `predictions(fit, newdata = grid, conf_level = 0.9)`. ::: ::: hint - For the line: a grid of state incomes from the poorest state to the richest, rescaled the same way as `rs_state_median_income`, with `income = 0`. - `re_formula = NA` sets every state's deviation to zero. ::: ::: sol **Part 1** ::: {.cell fit_deps='ces'} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_ces <- brm(vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name), data = ces, family = bernoulli, backend = "cmdstanr", iter = 10000, warmup = 2000, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit_ces) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Family: bernoulli Links: mu = logit Formula: vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name) Data: ces (Number of observations: 48582) Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 10000; warmup = 2000; thin = 1; total post-warmup draws = 32000 Multilevel Hyperparameters: ~state_name (Number of levels: 50) Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS sd(Intercept) 0.26 0.03 0.20 0.33 1.00 4993 9395 Regression Coefficients: Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Intercept -0.26 0.04 -0.33 -0.18 1.00 3211 income 0.01 0.01 -0.01 0.03 1.00 38723 rs_state_median_income -0.45 0.08 -0.60 -0.29 1.00 3305 Tail_ESS Intercept 6158 income 25269 rs_state_median_income 7113 Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1). ``` ::: ::: - R-hat 1.00 everywhere. Smallest bulk ESS above 2,000. Passes the notes' rule of thumb. **Part 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # one row per state; a voter in the middle income category grid <- mutate(states, income = 0) # pr(trump) with a 90% ci in each state p_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = grid, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() ``` ::: - Plot under Part 3, with the line. **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # state incomes from the poorest state to the richest, rescaled like rs_state_median_income line_grid <- tibble(state_median_income = seq(min(states$state_median_income), max(states$state_median_income), length.out = 50)) |> mutate(rs_state_median_income = (state_median_income - mean(states$state_median_income)) / (2 * sd(states$state_median_income)), income = 0) # a typical state: every state's deviation set to zero line_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = line_grid, re_formula = NA, conf_level = 0.9) |> as_tibble() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(p_ces, aes(x = state_median_income, y = estimate)) + geom_ribbon(data = line_ces, aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) + geom_line(data = line_ces) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0, color = "grey70") + geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr), size = 3) + labs(x = "State median household income ($1,000s)", y = "Pr(Trump) for a voter with income = 0\n(90% CI)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Part 4** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the two coefficients, with 90% intervals posterior_summary(fit_ces, variable = c("b_income", "b_rs_state_median_income"), probs = c(0.05, 0.95)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Est.Error Q5 Q95 b_income 0.011 0.008 -0.003 0.025 b_rs_state_median_income -0.446 0.079 -0.575 -0.316 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # one unit of rs_state_median_income is 2 sds of state median income ($1,000s) 2 * sd(states$state_median_income) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 24.76068 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # the line at the poorest and richest states line_ces |> slice(1, n()) |> select(state_median_income, estimate) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 state_median_income estimate 1 59.1 0.534 2 105. 0.335 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # each state's distance from the line: its estimate minus a typical state's at the same state income typical_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = grid, re_formula = NA) |> as_tibble() |> select(state_abbr, line = estimate) distance_ces <- p_ces |> select(state_abbr, estimate) |> left_join(typical_ces, by = "state_abbr") |> mutate(distance = estimate - line) |> arrange(desc(distance)) head(distance_ces, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # CES: Wyoming 0.612, Vermont 0.347. Both just outside the ANES CIs. ::: ## Ordered or Not? Gelpi and Paolino {ref="gelpi-paolino"} - March 2008 survey experiment on the war in Iraq (Gelpi; N = 1,000). - Each respondent read a short news story: successful military events in Iraq, unsuccessful events, or neither. Separately, a confident statement from President Bush ("no doubt ... we will succeed"), a cautious statement, or neither. - Then: what do you think of a timetable for withdrawing all American troops from Iraq? - Paolino (2017): the answers are ordered. Ordered logit; the effects of the stories change linearly with approval of Bush. - Gelpi (2017): unordered. Multinomial logit, separately for each level of Bush approval. Paolino, Philip. 2017. "Surprising Events and Surprising Opinions: The Importance of Attitude Strength and Source Credibility." *Journal of Conflict Resolution* 61(8): 1795--1815. Gelpi, Christopher. 2017. "The Surprising Robustness of Surprising Events." *Journal of Conflict Resolution* 61(8): 1816--1834. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load data gelpi <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/gelpi-iraq.csv") ``` ::: - `timetable`: "What do you think about the policy of setting a timetable with a specific date for withdrawing all American troops from Iraq?" Strongly approve, somewhat approve, somewhat disapprove, or strongly disapprove. - `bush_approval`: approval of President Bush, from 0 (strongly disapprove) to 3 (strongly approve). - `pos_events`, `neg_events`: 1 if the story reported successful (or unsuccessful) military events. No one read both. - `pos_bush`, `neg_bush`: 1 if the story included the confident (or cautious) statement from Bush. No one read both. The code below orders the answers from most anti-war ("strongly approve" of a timetable) to most pro-war ("strongly disapprove"), and makes an unordered copy with "somewhat approve" as the baseline (as in Gelpi 2017). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gelpi_tt <- gelpi |> mutate(timetable = factor(timetable, levels = c("Strongly approve", "Somewhat approve", "Somewhat disapprove", "Strongly disapprove")), timetable_nominal = relevel(factor(timetable, ordered = FALSE), ref = "Somewhat approve")) |> drop_na(timetable, bush_approval) ``` ::: 1. Fit Paolino's ordered logit with `MASS::polr()`: `timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * bush_approval`. (A simplified version of the model in Paolino's appendix Table A26, without the party dummies.) 1. Fit Gelpi's multinomial logit with `nnet::multinom()`: `timetable_nominal ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * factor(bush_approval)`. (The same as Gelpi's four separate models, one for each level of Bush approval.) How many parameters does each model have? 1. For each model, use `comparisons()` to compute the effect of positive events (`pos_events` from 0 to 1) on the probability of each of the four answers, at each level of Bush approval. Set the other three treatments to 0. Plot the effects with their 95% CIs, with one panel for each level of Bush approval and both models in each panel. 1. Among strong Bush disapprovers (`bush_approval` = 0), how do positive events change the four probabilities in the multinomial logit? Could the ordered logit produce this pattern? How strong is the evidence for it? 1. Compare the two models with AIC and BIC. Which does each prefer? 1. Which model would you report? Why? ::: hint - `datagrid(model = fit, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0, pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3)` as `newdata`. - For the multinomial logit, add `type = "probs"`. - The `group` column holds the answer. ::: ::: hint For part 4: under the ordered logit, $\Pr(Y_i = 1) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_1 - \eta_i)$ and $\Pr(Y_i = 4) = 1 - \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_3 - \eta_i)$. What happens to each as $\eta_i$ increases? As $\eta_i$ decreases? ::: ::: sol **Part 1** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # paolino: ordered logit, each treatment interacted with bush approval fit_ordered <- MASS::polr(timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * bush_approval, data = gelpi_tt, Hess = TRUE) summary(fit_ordered) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: MASS::polr(formula = timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * bush_approval, data = gelpi_tt, Hess = TRUE) Coefficients: Value Std. Error t value pos_events 0.08298 0.1985 0.41796 neg_events -0.16464 0.1947 -0.84542 pos_bush -0.01505 0.1968 -0.07645 neg_bush 0.11826 0.1969 0.60055 bush_approval 1.09310 0.1270 8.60708 pos_events:bush_approval 0.17327 0.1440 1.20293 neg_events:bush_approval 0.13646 0.1419 0.96196 pos_bush:bush_approval 0.01084 0.1509 0.07183 neg_bush:bush_approval -0.32012 0.1389 -2.30452 Intercepts: Value Std. Error t value Strongly approve|Somewhat approve -0.5815 0.1794 -3.2407 Somewhat approve|Somewhat disapprove 0.9721 0.1802 5.3949 Somewhat disapprove|Strongly disapprove 2.0710 0.1915 10.8144 Residual Deviance: 2360.836 AIC: 2384.836 ``` ::: ::: **Part 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # gelpi: multinomial logit, a separate set of effects for each level of bush approval fit_multinomial <- nnet::multinom(timetable_nominal ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * factor(bush_approval), data = gelpi_tt, trace = FALSE) # number of parameters attr(logLik(fit_ordered), "df") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} attr(logLik(fit_multinomial), "df") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 60 ``` ::: ::: - Ordered logit: 12 (nine coefficients and three cutpoints). - Multinomial logit: 60 (3 equations × 5 coefficients × 4 levels of Bush approval). **Part 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # no other story, each level of bush approval grid_ordered <- datagrid(model = fit_ordered, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0, pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3) grid_multinomial <- datagrid(model = fit_multinomial, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0, pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3) # effect of positive events on each probability # (the multinomial logit returns bush_approval as a factor, so make both numeric) c_ordered <- comparisons(fit_ordered, variables = "pos_events", newdata = grid_ordered) |> as_tibble() |> mutate(bush_approval = as.numeric(as.character(bush_approval))) c_multinomial <- comparisons(fit_multinomial, variables = "pos_events", newdata = grid_multinomial, type = "probs") |> as_tibble() |> mutate(bush_approval = as.numeric(as.character(bush_approval))) # both models c_both <- bind_rows(list(`Ordered logit` = c_ordered, `Multinomial logit` = c_multinomial), .id = "model") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(c_both, aes(x = estimate, xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high, y = group, color = model)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 0.2) + facet_wrap(vars(bush_approval), nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) + scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(levels(gelpi_tt$timetable))) + # scale order, top to bottom scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.2, 0, 0.2)) + labs(x = "Effect of positive events on the probability (95% CI)", y = NULL, color = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](wk10-exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: **Part 4** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the strong disapprovers c_both |> filter(bush_approval == 0) |> select(model, group, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 5 model group estimate conf.low conf.high 1 Ordered logit Strongly approve -0.0189 -0.107 0.0695 2 Ordered logit Somewhat approve 0.00202 -0.00799 0.0120 3 Ordered logit Somewhat disapprove 0.00831 -0.0307 0.0473 4 Ordered logit Strongly disapprove 0.00852 -0.0316 0.0486 5 Multinomial logit Somewhat approve -0.117 -0.228 -0.00509 6 Multinomial logit Strongly approve 0.0604 -0.0493 0.170 7 Multinomial logit Somewhat disapprove -0.0111 -0.0983 0.0760 8 Multinomial logit Strongly disapprove 0.0675 0.00117 0.134 ``` ::: ::: - Multinomial logit: Pr(somewhat approve) falls by 0.12 (95% CI from −0.23 to −0.005). Pr(strongly disapprove) rises by 0.07 (from 0.001 to 0.13). Pr(strongly approve) rises by 0.06 (from −0.05 to 0.17). Out of the middle, toward *both* ends. - The ordered logit can't do this. - As $\eta_i$ increases, $\alpha_1 - \eta_i$ and $\alpha_3 - \eta_i$ both decrease. $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}$ is increasing, so $\Pr(Y_i = 1)$ falls and $\Pr(Y_i = 4)$ rises. - As $\eta_i$ decreases, both reverse. - A treatment shifts $\eta_i$ by the same amount for everyone at a level of Bush approval, so its effects on the two end categories have opposite signs (or are both zero). - Ordered logit here: −0.02 on "strongly approve" and 0.01 on "strongly disapprove." - Weak evidence. The pattern depends on the rise in "strongly approve," and that interval includes zero. **Part 5** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(model = c("Ordered logit", "Multinomial logit"), parameters = c(attr(logLik(fit_ordered), "df"), attr(logLik(fit_multinomial), "df")), log_lik = c(logLik(fit_ordered), logLik(fit_multinomial)), aic = c(AIC(fit_ordered), AIC(fit_multinomial)), bic = c(BIC(fit_ordered), BIC(fit_multinomial))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 model parameters log_lik aic bic 1 Ordered logit 12 -1180. 2385. 2444. 2 Multinomial logit 60 -1146. 2413. 2707. ``` ::: ::: - Multinomial logit: 34 more in log-likelihood for 48 more parameters. - AIC (2,385 vs. 2,413) and BIC (2,444 vs. 2,707) both prefer the ordered logit. **Part 6** - No single right answer. Ours: the ordered logit, with the multinomial logit as a check. - AIC and BIC prefer it. - The one pattern it can't produce rests on an interval that includes zero. - 118 to 450 respondents per level of Bush approval: the multinomial logit's 60 parameters are imprecise. Notice its wider intervals in the plot. :::
